Most people in Iraq are not Sunni, but there’s an Arab Sunni elite, and there are then other groups. And what we now call Turkey is also a successor state. It’s carved out of the Ottoman empire, too, and it’s defined as a national state with Turkish as its language. It changes the name of its capital city from the Greek Constantinople to the kind-of-Greek Istanbul—which is also Greek, I understand, but it sounds more Turkish even though it’s Greek in origin. So we have these now-new states. And the Arab states and the new Turkish national state, they begin eliminating their minorities one by one by one. Montefiore: That’s correct. And so, you know, in Turkey, for example what happens, the new Turkish state is really defined on what we would now call, in progressive parlance, an ethno-religious basis. In the sense that Turks were Ottoman subjects who spoke Turkish, lived in what was regarded as the Turkish heartland, and were Muslim. And people who were Christian could not be Turkish. So what we see today—and it started with Atatürk’s version of Turkishness, but his was secular and this is religious. So that’s exactly right. And so they drove out the Armenians who had challenged them and tried to carve out a state in the east, and then they turned on the Greeks. And the Greeks—it was slightly a different story, because the Greeks had been promised a sort of new Byzantine Empire in what is now western Turkey. And the reason why they claimed that was because there were huge Greek Orthodox populations in western Turkey—that used to be called Ionia—that had been there for thousands of years, literally since the Trojan Wars. And they lived in cities like Smyrna, the great Greek city of Smyrna. And so now Greek armies arrived, backed by the British and the French—and this was an example of European interference in the region—they arrived to protect their own ancient local Greek populations, but also to increase their kingdom. The Greek kingdom, the Greek state. And there they encountered Atatürk and his new Turkish army. And what ensued was a brutal nation-building war of ethnic purging, population swaps. Brutal, huge battles of regular armies. The armies in this were huge. They were 150,000 strong each in these major battles, with artillery, of course, and everything. So they were real World War I battles. But this is in 1922, and the Turks won these battles, and they then drove out, massacring and driving and deporting the Greek populations of what is now western Turkey. And in 1923, the Treaty of Lausanne, which involved Britain and Greece, the populations were swapped. So all the Muslims went to Turkey, all the Christians were expelled— Frum: That sounds so antiseptic. Montefiore: It’s not that antiseptic, because there were huge massacres. Frum: It’s murder, it’s pillage, it’s people standing on docks. It’s cities on fire. Montefiore: Yeah. It’s people jumping into docks and drowning. It’s burning cities. And at the heart of it is the inferno of Smyrna, which is one of the most apocalyptic urban demolitions of all time. And this creation of the Turkish nation is so important, because it explains what we’re seeing now in the rise of Turkey as a regional power. And it explains both the militaristic Turkish nationalism. It explains also the aspiration for much more influence, the grievance that they were diminished inside these borders agreed on in 1923, and the wish to expand and re-energize the Ottoman idea. And that is what we’re seeing now with President [Recep Tayyip] Erdogan. Frum: Let me take you now to the Arabic-speaking countries, mostly Sunni, that are carved out of the Ottoman empire. Now, Egypt was notionally part of the Ottoman empire in the 19th century. It was really an independent state with a lot of British influence, some French influence. Egypt remains a reasonably cosmopolitan place after the First World War with Greek minorities, Jewish minorities. Syria has more French influence. Lebanon has a lot of French influence. Palestine, which is reserved as a Jewish homeland, is a British mandate. But there’s this new country of Iraq created, and it becomes kind of genocide central in the Arabic-speaking Middle East. Tell us about the history of Iraq from the end of the First World War to the advent of the Second World War. Montefiore: Well, that’s right. But the Egypt you described was—and it’s hard to imagine now—but Egypt was the most cosmopolitan country in the Middle East. The fellahin, the lower, you know, the peasant class, were Arab, but the merchant classes were—as you said, David—Jewish, Lebanese, Greek, Italian. And they were large populations. The Jewish population was several hundred thousand just on its own, and they were the descendants of Jews who had been settled in Egypt by Alexander the Great and the Ptolemies, so they’d been there for millennia. And the wealth of Egypt depended on this mercantile class. And then the ruling class, the landowners, were Turco-Circassians, who were the descendants of enslaved Christians who had been enslaved and kidnapped by the Ottomans and previous rulers from their villages. They were Christian children who’d been enlisted in the Ottoman or Mamluk armies, who had been stolen from their parents, who were probably murdered. And who had then been converted to Islam, manumitted, and then joined the army and founded these families, these dynasties. It’s just a fascinating story. And even in the 1920s, these people, the Turco-Circassians, were still owning and ruling Egypt. And the ruling kings of Egypt, as they became, were also Turco-Albanian dynasty, who didn’t even speak Arabic right into the 1930s, which is fascinating. So that’s Egypt. And so you’re absolutely right that these are incredibly complicated because of Ottoman countries. When you come to Syria and Lebanon, these are also multiethnic, multi-sectarian countries—as they still are, which is why their rulers to this day are desperately struggling to make them work as single countries. And the French mandate was for Greater Syria, which is now divided into Syria and Lebanon. But it’s just worth remembering how different these countries could have been. Because when one thinks of them as they were bound to be Syria and Lebanon, no, that isn’t how it worked at all. And that’s also true with Iraq. With Syria and Lebanon, the French were thinking about dividing it into five or six countries. And those countries were two Sunni ones in Aleppo and Damascus, and then a Druze one, an Alawite one at Latakia on the coast. And then they were going to devise a Christian Maronite country that the Christians would rule, who were the French allies in Lebanon. And in the end, they decided not to do this, but to divide it into two big countries: Syria and Lebanon. So then we get to Iraq. Again, one thinks of Iraq as set, but Iraq was known to the allies as Mesopotamia—“the land between the rivers” in Greek. Iraq was an old Arab name for this region, but there’d never been a country called Iraq before, just as there’d never been a country called Lebanon or Syria or Jordan. And these countries were all drawn by the Western overlords, particularly Britain and France. And Iraq was just a combination of three provinces, or vilayets, put together by the British. And the vilayets were Basra, Baghdad, and Mosul. And Mosul is where the oil was, and that’s the Kurdish area. And there was a big question as to whether Mosul would be in Iraq or not. And that’s a pretty important detail, because it’s partly the Kurdish area; it’s where the oil is. And the Turks, who we were just discussing a minute ago, wanted Mosul and believed Mosul should be in Turkey. Now, that would have really changed the situation. But the Western allies also wanted to create a state—not just for the Armenians that we were discussing, but for the Kurds. And the Kurds would have a state that was partly in what is now Turkey and partly in what is now Iraq. But that didn’t happen either, because the Kurds were betrayed by everybody. And talk about genocide; this is another genocide in the 1930s where Atatürk and the Turkish Republic bombed Kurdish revolts, destroyed Kurdish village, killed something like 40,000 to 50,000 using poison gas, bombing villages. And they crushed the Kurds for another generation. In Iraq, they hoped to get Mosul or at least to prevent a Kurdish state being created. And in the end, the British were determined that Mosul would stay in the new country they’d created of Iraq. But as you said, David, Iraq was a multiethnic, multinational, multi-sectarian country. It had a small Shia majority, a barely Sunni minority. But that minority was very educated—was the landowners, was the civil servants. And it had been favored and empowered by the Turks, who were also Sunni. And then there were huge minorities of Kurds, small Christian sects, the Chaldeans, and Assyrians. And when I say “small,” they were a million people, so they weren’t that tiny. Non-Muslim sects like the Yazidis and Turkmen and all sorts of other minorities. Assyrians who were Christian. Frum: And Jews in Baghdad. Montefiore: And Jews in Baghdad. And a third of Baghdad was Jewish. Yeah. And many of the great families there like the Sassoons, most famously, who later went to England and became the sort of richest family in England, basically. The Sassoons, “the Rothschilds of the East,” they were known as. They were an incredibly prosperous minority, and they dominated the city in many ways. And the most kind of privileged of them ran huge business empires and also served the Pashas who ran Baghdad and— Frum: And between 1919 and 1942, there’s just attack after attack on each of these groups: on the Assyrian Christians, on the Kurds, on the Jews. And they are murdered and driven into exile. Montefiore: That’s exactly what happened. One of the big outrages is in the early ’30s, when they turn on the Christian Assyrians and massacre them. The Assyrians flee the country. And it’s really the first sign in Iraq that these new nation-states created for the Arabs are actually contradicting the multiethnic kind of cosmopolitan nature of these regions, that had been, perhaps in some ways, at various moments—and one mustn’t generalize—better ruled by empires with capitals far away. And so the climax for the Jews comes in 1941 with the Farhud, which is a terrifying pogrom. But in these pogroms against the Jews in 1941, influenced by specifically Nazi propaganda and perpetrated by a self-consciously Nazi-influenced militia, it was an episode more like October the 7, you know—where women were raped and then their bodies mutilated. Body parts were paraded through the town. And it really took place at an interesting moment when the British were about to retake Baghdad, and a pro-Nazi government was just in the process of being overthrown in 1941. And in that interim period, they decided they were going to get the Jews, and they went round the town marking the doors of every Jewish house. And so when the Farhud started, when the pogrom started, they knew exactly the houses, and they could see the mark on the door. Which is just a sort of chilling detail, isn’t it, David? David Frum: Yeah. I want to bring now the story up to the present in our last few minutes. One of the things I think that you will hear said a lot on modern university campuses by advocacy groups of various kinds is—they’ll tell the story of this Edenic Middle East before the Jews got there, before the Jews came to the state of Israel. And they will ask, Why aren’t the Jews comfortable to live in a multiethnic, multinational state with an Arab majority? What could possibly go wrong in such a situation? And I wanted to give people a tour of that. The story of the Middle East from the weakening of the Ottoman empire, as you say, in the late 19th century, beginning with the attacks on the Armenians, most bloodily in the 1890s and continuing, is: You either have a state, or you’re dead. Those are your choices in the Middle East. Montefiore: That’s right, and that is one of the themes of the book. And one of the themes of the book is to confront all of these Edenic myths, which even a cursory look at the facts and the history will show you is entirely legendary and has never existed. You know, it starts with the myth that the Ottoman empire was this kind of wonderful kumbaya, tolerant, poetry-spouting kind of a multicultural society. And that was never true. It was a conquest society built on the enslavement and kidnapping of Christian children. This isn’t some sort of story, by the way. This is how the Ottoman empire, it was how it was so successful. This tribute of children—which the Ottoman empire took from Christian villages in the Caucasus, in the Crimea, in southern Ukraine, and also in the Balkans—was how it was provided with talented, energetic manpower. And the women went into the harems. The boys went into the army or the civil service. And the women in the harems. The most lucky of them became queens. They became the wives of actual sultans. And she was typical, but of the luckiest of those. But for the boys, they became soldiers. They were forcefully converted to Islam. Once they were about to become officers, they were manumitted—in other words, freed from slavery—and then they were able to work up the military. And they were the army of the Ottoman empire that conquered this vast empire from the borders of Libya all the way to the borders of Iran. So that’s the first thing about the Ottoman empire. The second thing is: There was tolerance, provided you accepted the total supremacy of Islam and Sultan. And if you in any way challenged that political and religious supremacy, you were slaughtered. The history of the Ottoman empire is filled with massacres of minorities and Jews at regular intervals. And this goes on right into the 19th century, well before we get to the 1890s, where David started this discussion. But, you know, a typical example is in 1860; 25,000 Christians were massacred in Damascus in the 1860 event, which was one of the occurrences that brought the Western powers into the Ottoman empire. And we’ve seen how the Ottoman Empire ended, with a proto-Nazi genocide of entire races. And then you get into the creation of these states. If we look into the second half of the 20th century—where Syria, Iraq, and Lebanon, they all became independent—again, you see a similar pattern. Dictators from one sect or another protected and promoted their own group. Saddam Hussein, for example, protected the Sunni majority, even though he was from a very poor Tikriti peasant family, and brutally crushed the Shiites and the Kurds. And ultimately, to come back to your theme, this culminated in the attempted genocide of the Kurdish nation in Iraq. So, again and again, we have this pattern where if you don’t have a state, you’re nothing. And if you do have a state, the only way to enforce it is with autocracy or with repression. And that is the process by which, in my book, you’ll see over a century and a quarter we go from this wonderful efflorescence of sects and ethnicities. You go to this bleaker and bleaker and bleaker environment, and the Christians virtually vanish. So that in 2000, like 25 years ago, you still had a million Christians in Iraq. After the Islamist insurgency during the Iraq War, now there are 115,000 Christians in Iraq. So 900,000 of them have gone. So this is the picture. Frum: And this process of consolidation also leads to economic and technological failure. So Egypt—the cosmopolitan Egypt you describe of the 19th century—there was a large stock market in Alexandria. Egypt was a food exporter. Cotton exporter. Montefiore: Huge cotton industry. Frum: A big, big destination for foreign investment. The Suez Canal. Frum: That’s the story of every region. And this story is told as one that the West did to the Middle East, not as a story something the Middle East did to itself Montefiore: Agree. So does it sound like anywhere? Frum: Yeah. Well, you don’t have the Kingdom of Greece, or now the Republic of Greece, sponsoring endless terrorist attacks on Turkey. Montefiore: No. But you do have— Frum: And saying that Turkey has no right to exist, and it should all be Greece. Montefiore: No, and that’s one of the huge differences. No one criticizes, no one says it’s disgusting. What, you know—what is Turkish nationalism? Why should the Turks have nationalism? You know, it’s only Israeli nationalism that is constantly challenged. So, but that’s part of it. And the other country that’s very similar—but none of these countries are the same, but there are strong parallels—and the other one is, of course, the creation of Pakistan. Which has huge similarities, and is almost simultaneous with the creation of Israel in 1947. The difference between all three of these, one major difference, is how small the war was in 1948—the Nakba War, or the War of Independence, the War of Israeli Independence was. In Pakistan and India, the loss of life and the scale of deportation and displacement was just colossal. Obviously, India is huge, and there were 1 to 3 million people killed in that process. There were 12 to 14 million people displaced. And out of it came Pakistan—which, again, is an ethno-religious creation which had never existed before, ever, in history, as a result of a new nationalism. And out of it comes, again, not a democracy, but a new sort of nationalism with religious characteristics, a strong military ethos, and huge swaths of population. So the creation of Israel isn’t completely unique, is what I’m saying. Frum: Well, there’s one difference between the creation of Turkey, the creation of Pakistan, and the creation of Israel—that the creation of Israel is the one example that involves a uniquely despised people in the region. The product of exile from other regions, actually now turning out to be quite a successful state. So there’s not just all the things you describe—all the carnage, all the movements of population—but there’s an element of humiliation that is ineradicable. These are the people who are supposed to be absolutely at the bottom of the regional hierarchy. Montefiore: The other half of the parallel would be to the Armenians. But what was different with the Armenians was, the Armenians were much smaller number. Such was the genocide against them that they didn’t recover enough ever to gather the strength to create the states that they were promised. While the Jews did recover from the Holocaust, which they endured, and they did manage to create a state. So there are fascinating parallels here, which I know we don’t have time to go into in detail. But this is so interesting to talk about this. Frum: I want to touch on one last thing. Which is in this discussion, we have used the words genocide over and over again, and we’ve used them to describe very large-scale killing involving the elimination or near-elimination, and followed by expulsion of large numbers of people. Organized according to ideological programs, with a view of elimination. And they are practiced by the Ottomans; they are practiced by the Turkish successors to the Ottomans; they are practiced by the Arab-states successors to the Ottomans, especially Iraq. The genocide that everyone talks about, imagines they know about, is the war between Israel and Hamas in Gaza. That did not involve this scale of killing; that did not involve any kinds of expulsions and that leaves Gaza physically damaged, but its people still alive and in place. And maybe it’s just a gap in what we know. We don’t like to read history. It’s about old people. We don’t like to read about other countries. They don’t speak English. It involves books and not short-form videos. So there’s a lot about this that is off-putting to the modern consumer. But there is something strange about the willingness to remember, to imagine one genocide that didn’t happen and to forget all the genocides that did Montefiore: That’s right. When I think of the word genocide I think that, as a historian, my duty is not to forget the millions of people killed in these successive genocides in the Middle East that I cover in The Cauldron. And this really starts with the million Armenians. But it goes on all the way through—and we’ve touched on some of those stories—the Maronite Christians, the Pontic Greeks, the Ionian Greeks, and all the way through to the Yazidis under the ISIS terror in our very recent history. Saddam Hussein’s killing of the Kurds and using of poison gas to try and exterminate the Kurds. So I think we have an absolute duty to honor these people, and any degradation of the term genocide , which is a special word morally, historically, and legally—anything that degrades the experience of those people is an insult to the memory of these people who must be remembered. And it is our duty to remember them. And nowadays, I think the word has been so degraded; it’s just become a hyperbolic, ideological insult that has become meaningless and is used as much to describe a brutal war in Gaza as it is to describe the blockade of Cuba, for example. And it’s just become a word that we use to describe a bad war or something we don’t like, and that is an insult to the peoples who faced the real genocides in the Middle East, which are chronicled in this book. Frum: Well, it could be a little more sinister than that. Because if your national program, if your ideological program, requires the forgetting of what was done to the Armenians, to the Assyrians, to the Kurds—if that has to be obliterated—then you want to devalue the word. And a great way to devalue a word is to apply it to things that didn’t happen. And that not only indicts the people you want to indict, in this case the Israelis, but it absolves the people who implicitly want to be absolved. And it buries a memory that many people want buried. Frum: Simon, thank you so much for joining me today on The David Frum Show. Montefiore: Thank you so much for having me, David. [ Music ] Frum: Thanks so much to Simon Sebag Montefiore for joining me today for that fascinating discussion. As mentioned at the top of the program, my book this week is The Hidden Hand , by Warren Kinsella, [subtitled] The Information War and the Rise of Antisemitic Propaganda , just published. Warren Kinsella is a prominent Canadian journalist, active for many years in Canadian party politics. He’s a close associate of former Prime Minister Jean Chrétien. He has become passionately involved in recent years in Canada in the debate over the state of Israel and its detractors. Kinsella is very much a shoe-leather journalist. He’s not interested in big theories. He’s interested in getting to the bottom of stories. And The Hidden Hand is his attempt to take his microphone place by place and understand how is it that you have seen this extraordinary surge of anti-Semitic propaganda on the new social media. His big thesis is that this surge is not an organic phenomenon. It’s not that thousands and hundreds of thousands and millions of separate people all over the planet have spontaneously and individually decided to turn their social-media feeds into attacks on the state of Israel. But rather that something is happening here driven by political actors, many of them foreign, but even more worryingly, driven by the nature of social media itself. The algorithm here is taking on a kind of mind of its own, and we are all becoming the algorithm’s captives, and our brain functions are becoming its product. We are moving into a world—and this is a theme I’ve often stressed in these book talks—that is less committed to the word and more to the image. Less committed to rational thought; more committed to emotional action, to emotional response. And therefore more susceptible to manipulation, both by people who want to manipulate and by machines that exist simply to cultivate engagement and to get people to feel anger and upset as a way to maximize engagement. We are building a political culture that is anti-rational, and anti-rational cultures are cultures that are very prone to conspiracy theories, which function as a kind of pseudo-rationality. They seem to explain the world even though they really don’t. And when you become connected to conspiracy theories, at the bottom of all conspiracy theories is the master conspiracy theory about the Jews. The Jews form an important part of the consciousness of ancient myths of Christianity, the killers of Christ; ancient myths of Islam, to deny that the people in the Bible were actually Muslims all along, and the Jews then falsely claim that Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, and so on were Jews when they were in fact Muslims all along, and so the Jews are falsifiers of their own scripture. And Jews also play an important part in the conspiracy theories of the third great Western religion, Marxism, where Jews are the people who are the ultimate expressions of the false consciousness: the attempt to hold onto religious and national identity instead of the true identity that Marxism wishes us all to embrace, the identity of class. As the target of all three of these kinds of conspiracy theories—in a time when conspiracy theories are emancipated and run wild—well, naturally the Jews occupy an enormous part in the consciousness of the conspirator. And in the images that you see on social media formed to buy and to win appeal, win audience from people prone to conspiracy theories. That’s Kinsella’s story. It’s a very disturbing one, and I recommend the book to people who want to understand what is happening and begin the work of understanding why and what to do about it. That’s it for this week’s David Frum Show. Thanks so much for watching or listening. Hope to see you again next week. Remember, the best way to support this program and all of us at The Atlantic is by subscribing to The Atlantic. I hope you will consider doing that. Share, like, and subscribe to this show on whatever platform you use. See you next week. Bye-bye. [ Music ]

items.title: Le Tchad présente à la Banque mondiale ses exigences pour réussir la transformation numérique
items.description: © (DR) Le ministre des Télécommunications, Haliki Choua Mahamat et le représentant de la Banque mondiale au Tchad, Farouk Mollah Banna ont eu des échanges relatif au Projet d’Appui à la transformation numérique et aux perspectives de partenariat. Un aperçu des réalisations faites au Tchad par la Banque Mondiale à travers des projets dans le le secteur des Télécommunications a été fait. Le ministre tchadien a relevé certaines insuffisances dans la mise en œuvre du Projet d’Appui à la transformation du Tchad (PATN). Il en ressort que, 500 sites devront être réalisés dans le cadre dudit projet. Haliki Choua Mahamat souhaite que ces installations techniques soient déployées dans les zones blanches (zone hors réseau) afin de permettre une connectivité. Il évoque également le fait que, le maillage sur le territoire national n’est pas complet. « Six provinces ne sont pas encore connectées par fibre optique » et qu’il faudra encore 8000 Km fibre optique pour un maillage total. Le ministre des Télécommunications déclare que : « sans connectivité totale, on ne pourra atteindre les objectifs de digitalisation et de transformation numérique. » Le membre du gouvernement a également fait un plaidoyer en faveur du Programme régional d’intégration numérique de l’Afrique centrale. Un plaidoyer orienté dans le cadre de l’appui institutionnel et la disposition des experts qualifiés au profit du ministère pour la réalisation des études et des cadres juridiques. Il a également sollicité l’appui de la Banque Mondiale pour la dotation en laboratoires modernes en intelligence artificielle à l’Ecole nationale supérieure des technologies de la Communication (ENASTIC), de l’Université de N’Djamena. Le ministère en charge des Télécommunications estime que, la Banque mondiale, par son représentant apprécie les échanges. Farouk Mollah Banna a : « a éclairé l’assistance ainsi que le Ministre sur les actions éligibles au niveau des portefeuilles de son institution et rassurant de la disponibilité de la Banque Mondiale à appuyer le Tchad dans sa transformation numérique. » L’article Le Tchad présente à la Banque mondiale ses exigences pour réussir la transformation numérique est apparu en premier sur Journal du Tchad .

Etats-Unis: le Congrès américain accentue la pression pour mettre fin à la guerre contre l’Iran
items.description: ETATS-UNIS-IRAN-GUERRE-CONGRES-PRESSION Etats-Unis: le Congrès américain accentue la pression pour mettre fin à la guerre contre l’Iran Ouagadougou, 16 sept. 2026 (AIB)- la Chambre américaine des représentants a adopté, mardi 15 septembre 2026, par 220 voix contre 204, une résolution demandant au président Donald Trump de retirer les forces américaines des opérations militaires contre l’Iran non autorisées par le Congrès. Le texte, adopté pour la troisième fois par la Chambre depuis le début du conflit, a recueilli les voix de l’ensemble des démocrates présents et de sept républicains. Lors des deux précédents votes à la Chambre, seuls quatre élus républicains avaient soutenu une initiative similaire. La résolution s’appuie sur le « War Powers Act », une loi adoptée après la guerre du Vietnam pour encadrer le recours du président aux forces armées et rappeler le rôle du Congrès dans l’autorisation des opérations militaires prolongées. La Chambre avait déjà adopté des résolutions similaires en juin puis en juillet 2026. Au Sénat, une résolution visant à mettre fin à la guerre avait également été approuvée, mais n’avait pas pu aboutir, faute de soutien suffisant des sénateurs républicains. Le coût de la guerre dépasse désormais 38 milliards de dollars, selon le Congressional Budget Office (CBO), qui estime les dépenses supplémentaires à environ trois milliards de dollars par mois en cas de poursuite des opérations. Parallèlement au vote de la Chambre, le représentant républicain Thomas Massie a déposé mardi une procédure de mise en accusation contre le secrétaire à la Défense Pete Hegseth, l’accusant d’avoir ordonné des opérations militaires contre l’Iran sans autorisation du Congrès. Le Pentagone a rejeté ces accusations et réaffirmé son soutien au secrétaire à la Défense. La question de la guerre intervient à l’approche des élections de mi-mandat prévues le 3 novembre 2026, qui détermineront notamment le contrôle des deux chambres du Congrès. La poursuite des hostilités pèse aussi sur les prix de l’énergie et l’inflation aux Etats-Unis. Agence d’Information du Burkina Source : RT

items.title: ‘New pathway for the future’: Quantum Valley Pakistan launched in Islamabad
items.description: Quantum Valley Pakistan, a project likened to America’s Silicon Valley, was launched in Islamabad on Wednesday, with Federal Minister for Planning, Development and Special Initiatives Ahsan Iqbal as the chief guest. The Planning Ministry described Quantum Valley Pakistan as a project aimed at connecting academia, entrepreneurs, government and investors to turn “knowledge into solutions, startups into scalable ventures and innovation into national impact”. The project aims to create new pathways for Pakistani talent in AI, quantum computing, fintech, agritech, biotechnology, medtech, digital solutions and autonomous technologies, the ministry said. California’s venture capital firm Plug and Play and the Cambridge Innovation Centre collaborated with the government for the project. Addressing the launch ceremony, Iqbal said, “We are actually setting a new pathway for Pakistan’s future”. “Pakistan is ready for innovation takeoff,” he said. He stressed that this was not an ordinary collaboration, adding that the two companies would bring to Pakistan the “best of innovation in the world and the United States”. Describing the collaboration as a “unique opportunity” for Pakistan, Iqbal expressed hope for the growth of the country’s technology sector. He said that the paradigm of national progress had shifted in the 21st century, with “brain power” now being a key requirement for development. The planning minister added that the foundations for growth being established through Quantum Valley would allow Pakistan’s youth to compete with the youth of the world in terms of tech growth and startups. “Today, we stand at an inflection point,” Iqbal said, adding that in the past two years, Pakistan had seen many successes, namely Marka-i-Haq and recent diplomacy efforts in the US-Iran war . “In my lifetime, I had never seen that for an entire week, media from the US to Australia was only mentioning Islamabad,” he said, referring to the Islamabad talks in April. Successes achieved in defence and diplomacy, if not supplemented by a strong economy, can blur over time, Iqbal said. Alluding to Marka-i-Haq , Iqbal said the nation had to rise to the occasion of “ Marka-i-Taraqi ” and aim to build a $1 trillion economy by 2035 under the Uraan Pakistan programme. He further said the economy should grow to $3 trillion by 2047, when the country marks its centenary. Uraan Pakistan is an initiative of the Planning Ministry designed to advance key projects and reforms set out in the 5Es National Economic Transformation Plan. “These goals are ambitious but not impossible,” Iqbal said. Iqbal urged the nation to move away from the status quo and instead opt for a “transformational path”. The ceremony also included the inauguration of the Global Venture Acceleration Programme for local startups, under which they would receive mentorship over 15 weeks, along with a two-week global immersion in Silicon Valley or Boston.
